title: Renunciation vs relinquishment (18.1–18.12)
hook: the last chapter opens with Arjuna asking the difference between two kinds of giving up
carry: let go of the fruit, not the act

segments.voice: Yesterday, om tat sat: begin with the sound, offer it to that, let it be real and good. Today, the Gita's last chapter, the graduation chapter.

Some people, when life gets hard, want to walk away from all of it. Quit the job, delete the apps, move to a cabin, done. And some people keep showing up to everything, but inside they've quietly stopped needing it to go their way. From the outside, the first one looks like the spiritual one. Chapter eighteen begins with Arjuna asking about exactly this. It's his last question in the whole Gita, and it goes all the way back to where he started: wanting to drop his bow and walk off the field.
screen: `WALK AWAY FROM IT ALL?` → `OR STAY, AND STOP GRIPPING?` → `ARJUNA'S LAST BIG QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Verse one: Arjuna asks to know the truth of two words. Sannyasa, renunciation, and tyaga, relinquishment. Both mean giving up. Verse two: the wise say sannyasa is giving up actions done out of desire. And tyaga, they say, is giving up the fruit of all actions. Verse three admits people disagree. Some thinkers say all action has faults, so give it all up. Others say sacrifice, giving and discipline should never be given up. Then Krishna gives his own view, verse five: sacrifice, giving and discipline should not be abandoned. They should be done. They purify the wise. Verse six: but even these should be done without attachment, and without clinging to the fruit. This is my firm conclusion. Then the three threads come back, now applied to giving up. Verse seven: quitting your proper duty out of confusion is tamasic. Verse eight: quitting because it's hard, or you're afraid of the strain, is rajasic, and it gets you nothing. Verse nine: doing your duty because it should be done, while letting go of attachment and the fruit, that's sattvic relinquishment. Verse eleven says it plainly. No one with a body can give up action completely. But the one who gives up the fruit of action is called a relinquisher. So the Gita's answer to the man who wanted to throw down his bow is not walk away. It's stay, act, and let go of the outcome: chapter two's teaching, now in its final form.
screen: `SANNYASA AND TYAGA.` · `DON'T DROP THE GOOD WORK.` · `QUITTING FROM FEAR GETS NOTHING.` · `NO ONE CAN STOP ACTING.` · then, large: `RENUNCIATION VS RELINQUISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Think of one duty you'd love to quit, something that's yours to do but heavy, and notice whether the urge to drop it is confusion or fear of the strain. Then, without deciding anything, picture doing it tomorrow, fully, but without needing it to turn out a particular way. Feel the difference in your shoulders; that's relinquishment.
Tyaga, relinquishment, letting go. Gita eighteen: sannyasa gives up actions; tyaga gives up the fruit, and Krishna's firm conclusion is to keep acting and let go of the fruit.
Your line: let go of the fruit, not the act. Stay on the field, and loosen the grip. Two hundred nineteen days, and counting.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors sannyasis, renunciants who leave household life, and it also teaches householders the Gita's tyaga: doing one's duties fully while letting go of attachment to results.

match.prompt: two kinds of giving up — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna, at the start of the last chapter. you've wanted to drop your bow since chapter one. what's Krishna's firm conclusion?
options: keep acting, without attachment or clinging to the fruit.
act only when you're sure of the result.
fork.reveal: verse 6: even sacrifice, giving and discipline should be done without attachment to the fruit. that's his firm conclusion.

original.note: Sanskrit: tyaga, relinquishment, letting go; in Gita 18, giving up the fruit of action, not the action.

trapdoor: what you thought: the spiritual move is to quit everything.
what it means: the Gita says keep doing what's yours to do, and let go of the fruit.
what a scholar hears: 18.2 distinguishes sannyasa (giving up kamya karma, desire-driven acts) from tyaga (giving up karma-phala); 18.7–18.9 sort tyaga by the three gunas.
guess: letting go of the results while still acting
leaving home and family for a monk's life
giving away all your money to the poor
